problem: “usually attributed” softened to “usually expected” and “very widely” lost its intensifier; keep his wording.
replacement: I have already noted that universal suffrage has been adopted in all the States of the Union. It therefore operates among populations that hold very different positions on the social scale. I have had the chance to observe its effects in different places, and among peoples who are almost strangers to one another in language, religion, and way of life: in Louisiana as in New England, in Georgia and in Canada. I have noticed that universal suffrage is far from producing in America either all the good or all the evil consequences that people in Europe assign to it, and that its effects differ very widely from those usually attributed to it.

problem: Garbled comma placement and grammar in “to believe, without saying so, or to say, without believing it”.
replacement: Many people in Europe tend to believe without saying so, or to say without believing, that one of the great advantages of universal suffrage is that it puts the direction of public affairs in the hands of men who deserve the public’s confidence. They admit that the people cannot govern itself, but they assert that it is always sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of the State, and that it instinctively picks out those who share its good intentions and are best fit to hold supreme authority. I confess that what I observed in America does not agree with these opinions at all. When I arrived in the United States I was surprised to find so much distinguished talent among the governed and so little among the heads of the government. It is a well-established fact that today the ablest men in the United States are very rarely placed at the head of affairs, and it must be acknowledged that this has come about as democracy has overstepped all its former limits. The breed of American statesmen has clearly declined remarkably over the last fifty years.

problem: “vulgar demeanor” became “unrefined appearance”; demeanor (behavior, bearing) shifted to looks.
replacement: There are, however, certain laws of a democratic nature that help to correct, to some extent, the dangerous tendencies of democracy. On entering the House of Representatives in Washington, one is struck by the unrefined demeanor of that great assembly. The eye often fails to find a famous man within its walls. Its members are almost all obscure individuals whose names call nothing to mind: they are mostly village lawyers, tradesmen, or even people from the lower classes of society. In a country where education is very widespread, it is said that the people’s representatives do not always know how to write correctly.

problem: “the connections of the candidateship” rendered as “any restrictions attached to candidacy”, an interpretation that adds a specific claim (legal restrictions); keep it closer to the source.
replacement: I regard the complete absence of unpaid officials in America as one of the most prominent signs of the absolute dominion that democracy exercises there. All public services, of whatever kind, are paid, so that everyone has not merely the right but also the means to perform them. Although in democratic States all citizens are qualified to hold positions in the government, not all are tempted to seek them. The number and abilities of the candidates are more likely to limit the electors’ choice than any conditions attached to candidacy.

problem: Source says the magistrates exercise arbitrary power; candidate says the governments give it to them (a shift from exercise to grant), and the *a marker now collides with the article (“*a a considerable”).
replacement: In two different kinds of government the magistrates *a exercise a considerable degree of arbitrary power: under the absolute government of a single individual, and under that of a democracy. Nearly analogous causes produce this identical result.

problem: Added enumerators “First,” and “Second,” and recast “and those who” as a separate numbered reason; the source runs the two points together after “two striking reasons”.
replacement: But let us now suppose that legislative authority is vested in the lowest orders. Two striking reasons show that expenditure will tend to increase, not decrease. Since the great majority of those who make the laws own no property that can be taxed, all the money spent for the community appears to be spent to their advantage, at no cost to themselves; and those who do own some small property readily find ways to arrange the taxes so that they burden the wealthy and benefit the poor, whereas the rich cannot take the same advantage when they are in possession of the government.
